title: Precision, Recall & F1
interviewAnswer: Precision asks: of predicted positives, how many were correct? Recall asks: of actual positives, how many did we find? F1 is the harmonic mean and is useful when both matter, but the right metric depends on error costs.
keyPoints: False positive vs false negative cost
why: Precision/recall questions appear constantly in interviews because real systems rarely value false positives and false negatives equally.
intuition: For a “failure” detector, recall asks “of all actual failures, how many did we catch?” Precision asks “of all alerts, how many were truly failures?”
deepDive: Accuracy can look excellent on imbalanced data while the model detects nothing useful. Precision and recall change with the decision threshold. F1 summarizes both using a harmonic mean, but should not replace explicit thinking about business costs.
code:
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score, f1_score
y_true = [1,1,1,0,0,0,0,0]
y_pred = [1,1,0,1,0,0,0,0]
print(precision_score(y_true, y_pred))
print(recall_score(y_true, y_pred))
print(f1_score(y_true, y_pred))
commonMistakes: Choosing accuracy for a 1% positive class without checking class balance.
Saying “recall is true positives” without defining its denominator.
Selecting the threshold solely because precision and recall cross.
followUps: When is PR-AUC preferable to ROC-AUC?
How would you choose the threshold?
How do class weights affect training?
production: Monitor the metric at the operating threshold and across important slices. If labels arrive late, separate immediate system monitoring from delayed model-quality monitoring.
workedExample: For safety-critical failure detection, require a minimum recall first, then maximize precision among thresholds meeting that safety constraint.

lab.goal: Compute the confusion matrix metrics manually and with sklearn.
lab.buildIt:
y=[1,1,1,0,0,0]; pred=[1,0,1,1,0,0]
tp=sum(a==1 and b==1 for a,b in zip(y,pred)); fn=sum(a==1 and b==0 for a,b in zip(y,pred))
fp=sum(a==0 and b==1 for a,b in zip(y,pred))
precision=tp/(tp+fp); recall=tp/(tp+fn); f1=2*precision*recall/(precision+recall)
print(tp,fp,fn,precision,recall,f1)

visual.title: Confusion matrix
visual.caption: Precision focuses on positive predictions; recall focuses on actual positives. The matrix makes the error types explicit.
